newsitem.title: USA: Kevorkian charged with assisting suicides again.
newsitem.headline: Kevorkian charged with assisting suicides again.

text.p: Dr. Jack Kevorkian, the assisted-suicide crusader acquitted in three previous trials, was charged again on Thursday along with two others with crimes linked to 10 deaths since June.

The charges were approved by Oakland County Prosecutor Richard Thompson, who has weeks left in office after losing a primary battle to an opponent who said he thought it was a waste of taxpayer money to further pursue Kevorkian.
The retired 68-year-old pathologist branded Thompson a "lying psychotic" and referred to the court as a "Nazi court."
Kevorkian's lawyer Jeffery Fieger referred in court to Kevorkian's hunger strike during previous jail time on assisted suicide charges.
After the hearing before Judge Edward Avadenka, Kevorkian said he valued his liberty more than his life. "(Either) I die or the legal system gets out of this," he said.

In granting $50,000 bail, the judge overturned a ruling by a magistrate minutes earlier that Kevorkian's release be conditioned on him not assisting in any more suicides, and Kevorkian and Fieger marched out of the courtroom.
"This is not going to be the court that will make a martyr out of Dr. Kevorkian," Avadenka said, referring to the threat of a Kevorkian hunger strike.

Kevorkian has admitted helping 44 people die since 1990 and has been the leading U.S. advocate for physician-assisted suicide. He has been tried and acquitted three times on related charges since 1994.

The latest charges involve 10 suicides in which Kevorkian assisted since June 20, including the controversial July 9 suicide of Rebecca Badger. In that case the issue of whether Badger was terminally ill when she died was challenged by the medical examiner, who ruled her death a homicide.

Prosecutor Neil Rockind told reporters that the prosecution had a tape of Badger telling police in her native California in January that she did not want to end her life, but that she sometimes was depressed and susceptible to suggestions by her mother that she consider suicide.
After saying that she did not want her life to end, "she meets doctor Kevorkian and her life ends," Rockind said.
Charged along with Kevorkian in several of the assisted suicides were George Reding and Neal Nicol. Nicol's home was used in at least one assisted suicide.
Named as an unindicted coconspirator was Janet Good, a long-time Kevorkian ally and a founder of the Michigan Hemlock society who is terminally ill with pancreatic cancer.
Kevorkian, Reding and Nicol were also charged with moving the victims' bodies without permission of the medical examiner.

Kevorkian was also charged with possession of a controlled substance, listed as less than 25 grams of secobarbital, and with holding himself out to be a practicing physician while engaging in unlawful conduct. Kevorkian no longer has a medical license.

The U.S. Supreme Court this month let stand a Michigan Supreme court ruling that upheld an injunction barring him from using his assisted suicide machine, other devices or drugs to hasten a person's death.
"The Supreme Court cannot make law," Kevorkian said outside court.
Noting that Kevorkian has repeatedly violated that injunction, Rockind argued that if he was released on bond, Kevorkian would assist in other suicides.
Fieger argued that Kevorkian was not assisting suicides, but helping to end suffering.
